narration: On Earth, a flame heats the air around it. The hot gas rises, and fresh air rushes in to feed the fire. In orbit, nothing rises. A flame is fed only by the airflow the spacecraft provides. That changes how fires start, spread, and go out.

NASA has studied fire in microgravity for decades: on the International Space Station, on uncrewed cargo ships, in drop towers and on rockets. The results are scattered across test tables, figures and reports. This year's Space Apps challenge asks for an AI-powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets those findings for crews heading to the Moon and Mars.

MicroFire Atlas starts from NASA's own records. We transcribed fifty-six individual tests from the BASS-II summary report, keeping the original units and the crew's notes word for word. Every value is labelled: recorded for that test, stated for the whole series, or derived by us. Every quoted finding is checked against the original PDF text. If a quote does not match, the build fails.

Here is every test on one map: oxygen against airflow. Amber flames kept burning. Blue flames went out when the flow dropped. Pale ones were blown out. Now, three tests. The same thin acrylic film, at about sixteen and a half percent oxygen. In test B16 the fan was turned down, and the flame quenched. In B20, at moderate flow, it burned the entire sample. In B19, at ten centimeters per second, it blew out. The main difference was the airflow.

The fabric tests show the pattern from another angle. As oxygen fell from eighteen point seven to sixteen point nine percent, the flame went out at slightly higher airflow. NASA's researchers report quenching speeds between one and five centimeters per second, higher in lower oxygen.

At the lowest flows, below one centimeter per second, NASA saw flames turn dim blue and very stable, able to burn for a long time. The researchers warn that a tiny flame might go undetected, then flare up if the air suddenly moves.

Mission Lab turns this into a planner's question. Describe a cabin: oxygen, airflow, pressure and gravity. The atlas ranks every test by how closely it matches, and shows the arithmetic behind each score. Now switch to the exploration atmosphere NASA recommends for Moon and Mars missions: thirty-four percent oxygen at fifty-six and a half kilopascals. No test scores sixty or higher, and the atlas says so plainly: direct evidence under these exact conditions is limited.

The gap map shows where the evidence runs out. Every range above twenty-two percent oxygen is empty, and every test here ran in orbit near normal pressure. Partial-gravity data is scarce. NASA describes its LUCI rocket experiment as the first combustion tests longer than twenty-five seconds in simulated lunar gravity.

Ask a question, and the atlas first finds the matching tests and NASA quotes. Only that evidence goes to the language model. Each claim comes back labelled as observed, derived, interpretation or data gap, and is checked. Invented test numbers are removed. Numbers missing from the cited evidence are flagged.

MicroFire Atlas. Fifty-six NASA tests, nineteen verified findings, and an honest map of what we do not know. AI that helps scientists interrogate evidence, not AI that replaces it. Safer exploration begins by knowing what the evidence says, and where it stops.
